description: Automated YouTube Shorts pipeline - discovers strange historical events, generates scripts with Claude AI, creates images, records voiceover, assembles videos, and uploads to YouTube daily.
content:
Repository: poyrazemun/youtube-shorts-generator
    Description: Automated YouTube Shorts pipeline - discovers strange historical events, generates scripts with Claude AI, creates images, records voiceover, assembles videos, and uploads to YouTube daily.
    Language: Python
    Topics: claude-code, content-generation, python, youtube-automation-ai, youtube-shorts

    README:
    Unreal History Bot > An autonomous YouTube Shorts channel about strange real history. Run it on a daily schedule and the channel runs itself — topics, scripts, images, voiceover, subtitles, upload. 📺 See it in action: @ThatActuallyHappened11 on YouTube — the live channel this repo runs. You set it up once. From then on, one command per day publishes one short. Topics are picked from a Claude-generated queue scored for virality, scripts use proven hook formulas, images come from FLUX, the voice is ElevenLabs (or free Kokoro TTS), and YouTube performance data feeds back into the next batch of topics so the channel learns what works. --- Highlights - Virality-scored topic queue — Claude rates 25 topic ideas 1–10; only ≥7 ship, sorted best-first. - Content-safety pre-check — every script is evaluated against YouTube's demotion rules before any image-generation spend; failed scripts halt the pipeline and are marked failed in the queue. - Scene-aware image prompts — role + preset system, plus per-beat scenevisuals so the 5 images describe distinct moments (wide → close-up → portrait → action → aftermath) instead of 5 near-identical takes on one theme. - Manual image A/B mode — --manual-images pauses the pipeline after scene planning so you can drop in images from Midjourney / DALL-E / Sora / etc. and resume; lets you A/B test external generators against the FLUX baseline. See manual-usage.md. - Script review pause — --script-check halts the pipeline right after scripts.json is written so you can read the exact narration that will be spoken and fact-check / hand-edit it before any image-generation or TTS spend; press ENTER to reload the edited file and continue. - Multi-language metadata — title + description auto-translated to Spanish / Portuguese / Hindi / Indonesian via Haiku 4.5 and attached to the upload as YouTube localizations. - Real caption tracks — SRT uploaded via captions.insert, so the CC button in the YouTube player exposes a selectable English track (not just burned-in pixels). - Whisper-timed subtitles — burned-in 3-word cards synced to the audio, with a CTA overlay in the last 3 seconds. - Analytics feedback loop — --analytics summarises which keywords and hook types perform best; those signals are injected into the next --refresh-topics prompt. - Per-run cost + timing tracker — output/ /cost.json + a chronological costledger.txt with running totals. - Fully resumable — every step caches its output. Re-run after any failure and the pipeline picks up where it stopped. --- Table of Contents - Quick Start - How It Works - Requirements - Setup - CLI - Topic Virality Scoring - Content Safety Check (Step 2.5) - Cost & Timing Tracking - Analytics Feedback Loop - Hook Formulas - Daily Automation - Image / Voice Generation - Scene Planning & Presets - Output Format & Structure - Built With Claude Code --- Quick Start bash git clone && cd youtube-shorts-generator py -3.12 -m pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # then add ANTHROPICAPIKEY + REPLICATEAPITOKEN py -3.12 orchestrator.py --refresh-topics # generate the topic queue py -3.12 orchestrator.py --auto # publish one video Full setup (ffmpeg, espeak-ng, YouTube OAuth) is in Setup below. > The commands use py -3.12 (the Windows Python launcher). On macOS or Linux, replace it with python3.12 everywhere. --- How It Works The pipeline is a six-step CLI: pick a topic from the scored queue, write the script, generate images, synthesise voice, burn captions, upload. Every step caches its output, so re-running picks up where it stopped. Cost per video — measured from a real run (output/ /cost.json). These Claude steps run on every video: | Always-on (per video) | Cost | |---|---| | Claude — event + script + content safety (Sonnet 4.6) | $0.034 | | Claude — historical fact-check pass (Haiku 4.5, 750 in / 350 out) | $0.0025 | | Claude — localizations, title + description × 4 languages (Haiku 4.5) | $0.012 | | Captions, ffmpeg assembly, YouTube upload | Free | | Subtotal | $0.05 | Then you pick one image backend and one voice — these are either/or alternatives, not all required: | Pick one — image backend | Cost | |---|---| | HuggingFace FLUX.1-schnell (HUGGINGFACEAPITOKEN set) | Free | | Replicate FLUX.1-dev (5 × $0.025) | $0.125 | | Pick one — voice | Cost | |---|---| | Kokoro TTS (default, local) — also Piper / Coqui / Edge | Free | | ElevenLabs (optional, ELEVENLABSENABLED=true) | flat $5/mo subscription† | So a full run costs: $0.05/video with the free HuggingFace + Kokoro combo, or $0.17/video if you use Replicate for images. The voice choice doesn't change the per-video number (Kokoro is free; ElevenLabs is a flat monthly fee, below). † ElevenLabs Starter is a flat $5/mo plan (30,000 credits ≈ 54 videos on elevenmultilingualv2, 108 on a Flash model), not a per-render charge — so it doesn't appear in cost.json, which tracks only marginal API spend. Effective per-video cost is $5 ÷ videos-that-month (≈ $0.09–0.17 at a daily cadence). A monetized channel needs at least Starter for commercial rights anyway. See elevenlabs.md. HuggingFace images are free; the Replicate path is the safer fallback (no rate limits, consistent quality on FLUX.1-dev) but you pay per image. Detailed pipeline diagram --refresh-topics Claude generates 25 topics, scores each for viral potential (1-10), discards anything below 7, filters out already-used keywords, resets stale runs, sorts by score — best topics queued first ↓ --auto (run daily via Windows Task Scheduler) ↓ Step 1 eventdiscovery.py Claude → 1 strange historical event Step 2 scriptgenerator.py Claude + DuckDuckGo research → viral script with hook formula + rehook + loopable ending + per-beat scenevisuals + SEO metadata (accuracy guardrail: strict directive in the system prompt + a swift Haiku fact-check pass that corrects pop-history myths before saving) Step 2b localizer.py Haiku 4.5 → es/pt/hi/id title + description, cached in scripts.json Step 2.5 contentsafety.py Claude evaluates the script vs. YouTube demotion rules; halts before image spend on a fail Step 3 imagegenerator.py FLUX (HuggingFace schnell, or Replicate dev) → 5 cinematic 9:16 images Step 4 ttsgenerator.py ElevenLabs (if enabled) → Kokoro neural TTS → narration audio (fallback: Piper → Coqui → Edge TTS) Step 5a captions.py Whisper / estimation → word-timed subtitles Step 5b videoassembler.py ffmpeg → 1080×1920 MP4 with burned captions + CTA overlay + background music Step 6 youtubeuploader.py YouTube Data API v3 → upload video + SRT caption track + localized metadata ↓ --analytics Fetches view counts, feeds performance data back into topic generation --- Requirements - Python 3.12 (Kokoro TTS requires 3.10–3.12) - ffmpeg on PATH - espeak-ng on PATH (required by Kokoro) - Anthropic API key (Claude) - YouTube Data API v3 OAuth credentials - Replicate API token (for image generation, $0.025/image with FLUX.1-dev — see Cost) - (Optional) ElevenLabs API key + Starter plan ($5/mo) for premium hosted voice — else free Kokoro is used bash pip install -r requirements.txt bash Windows winget install ffmpeg macOS brew install ffmpeg Linux sudo apt install ffmpeg --- Setup 1. Environment bash cp .env.example .env env ANTHROPICAPIKEY=sk-ant-... REPLICATEAPITOKEN=r8... # $0.025/image with FLUX.1-dev (5 images = $0.125 per video) YOUTUBEPRIVACY=private Optional — premium hosted voice (else free Kokoro is used): ELEVENLABSENABLED=true # flat $5/mo Starter; omit/false to stay on Kokoro ELEVENLABSAPIKEY=sk... # elevenlabs.io → Settings → API Keys ELEVENLABSVOICEID=... # Voice Library → pick a voice → Copy Voice ID 2. YouTube API credentials - Google Cloud Console → Enable YouTube Data API v3 - Create OAuth 2.0 Client ID (Desktop app) → download as clientsecrets.json - Place in project root 3. First run (opens browser for YouTube OAuth) bash py -3.12 orchestrator.py --analytics --- CLI bash Automated mode — picks highest-scoring topic from queue, runs full pipeline py -3.12 orchestrator.py --auto Regenerate topic queue (Claude scores + filters 25 topics; run weekly to keep queue fresh) py -3.12 orchestrator.py --refresh-topics View current topic queue with virality scores py -3.12 orchestrator.py --list-topics Fetch YouTube analytics + print performance summary py -3.12 orchestrator.py --analytics Manual mode py -3.12 orchestrator.py --topic "Strange War Stories" --keyword "battle" [--count N] [--no-upload] Pick a specific topic from the queue by ID (shown in --list-topics) py -3.12 orchestrator.py --pick a3f2 Wipe entire queue and generate a fresh one (asks for confirmation) py -3.12 orchestrator.py --clear-topics Remove a single topic by ID (asks for confirmation) py -3.12 orchestrator.py --delete-topic a3f2 Dry run — validate pipeline wiring end-to-end with zero API spend (skips Claude, forces PIL images, skips YouTube upload; topic/keyword optional) py -3.12 orchestrator.py --dry-run Manual image mode — pause after scene planning so you can drop in images generated externally (Midjourney / DALL-E / Sora / etc.), then re-run the same command to resume from TTS through upload. See manual-usage.md. py -3.12 orchestrator.py --auto --manual-images Script check — pause right after scripts.json is written so you can read the exact narration that will be spoken in the video and fact-check / fix it by hand. Press ENTER to reload the edited file and continue. py -3.12 orchestrator.py --auto --script-check Flags available on all modes --no-upload skip YouTube upload, save videos locally --no-edit skip prompt editing pause (automation mode) --verbose DEBUG-level console logging --dry-run skip Claude + force PIL images + skip upload (no API spend) --manual-images pause after scene planning; resume once you have dropped img0..N.png into the printed folder --script-check pause after scripts.json is written so you can review/edit the spoken text, then ENTER to reload and continue --- Topic Virality Scoring Every time --refresh-topics runs, Claude rates each generated topic on a 1–10 virality scale: | Score | Meaning | |---|---| | 9–10 | Sounds completely fake but is true. Debunks a widely-held belief. Famous person in shocking context. | | 7–8 | Genuinely surprising with strong hook potential. | | < 7 | Discarded — not queued | Topics are sorted highest score first, so --auto always produces the most viral-potential video available. Deduplication Keywords from already-uploaded videos (tracked in videoregistry.json) are automatically excluded during topic generation — both via the Claude prompt and a post-generation filter. This prevents the pipeline from regenerating videos on topics you've already covered. Stale Run Recovery If a pipeline run crashes or is interrupted, the topic stays inprogress. On the next --refresh-topics, any inprogress entry older than 2 hours is automatically reset to failed and replaced with fresh topics. Content Safety Check (Step 2.5) Between script generation and image generation, every script is run through one Claude call that evaluates it against growth/youtube-restriction-rules.md. If the script would be demoted, age-restricted, demonetized, or removed by YouTube — most importantly Rule 4 (conspiracy framing), Rule 5 (forbidden categories: suicide methods, sexual violence, harm to minors, terrorism glorification, false claims about living people), and Rule 6 (graphic gore as focal point) — the pipeline halts before spending on image generation. The topic is marked failed in the queue with the violated rule, so re-running --auto picks the next pending topic. The full per-script verdict is saved to output/ /safety.json for audit. Safety check failures on infrastructure (Claude API down, malformed JSON response) fail-open with a warning — only a successful "fail" verdict from Claude halts the run, so an offline Claude doesn't block your pipeline. The check is skipped under --dry-run (zero API spend stays zero). Cost & Timing Tracking Every successful run records per-step wall-clock + Claude token usage + image-generation counts (per provider) and writes two artifacts: - output/ /cost.json — full breakdown for that one video (steps, timings, tokens, image counts, USD totals). Tracks marginal API spend only (Claude tokens + per-image provider charges); flat subscriptions like ElevenLabs TTS ($5/mo) are not included since they aren't per-render. - output/costledger.txt — chronological one-line-per-video append-only log with a TOTAL footer recomputed each run. Re-running the same slug replaces the existing row instead of duplicating it. Both files are gitignored. After each successful run a one-line summary prints to the console: Pipeline finished in 127s, $0.1736 spend (Claude $0.0486, images 5×replicate $0.1250) The Claude figure aggregates every Claude call in the run — Sonnet (event, script, safety) plus the Haiku fact-check and localization passes. Dated model IDs (e.g. claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) are normalized to their CLAUDEPRICING base key, so Haiku spend is costed correctly rather than logged as $0. Updating pricing when rates change Pricing rates live in config.py: - CLAUDEPRICING — {modelid: {"input": $/MTok, "output": $/MTok}}. If Anthropic changes prices or you switch models, edit the dict directly. Unknown models are recorded as $0 (with a warning logged), so an unset model won't crash a run. - IMAGEPRICING — {provider: $/image}. Replicate and HuggingFace rates are also env-overridable via IMAGECOSTREPLICATE and IMAGECOSTHUGGINGFACE in .env, so you can tweak rates without touching code. Switching image providers If you swap providers (e.g. Replicate → HuggingFace, or add a new one), update both: 1. The actual provider call in pipeline/imagegenerator.py (detectbackend() and the per-backend functions). 2. IMAGEPRICING in config.py — add the new provider's per-image cost so cost tracking stays accurate. The provider key recorded into cost.json is whatever string imagegenerator passes to tracker.recordimage(), so keep the names aligned. Analytics Feedback Loop --analytics fetches view/like counts for every uploaded video and saves them to output/analytics.json along with two derived signals (each requires ≥ 2 videos to be considered, so single uploads can't poison the ranking): - Top / worst keywords — average views grouped by keyword - Hook type performance — average views grouped by the hooktype Claude tagged on each script The next time --refresh-topics runs, those signals are flattened into a plain-English hint string and injected into Claude's topic-generation prompt — for example: "Top performing keywords by average views: napoleon (12,400 avg, 3 videos). Hook type performance: FALSEASSUMPTION (9,800 avg, 4 videos). Prefer FALSEASSUMPTION hooks when it fits the story." Claude is told to bias new topics toward winning patterns and avoid losing ones. The exact hint string Claude received is persisted into topicsqueue.json as performancehintsused, so you can audit afterwards which signal shaped the queue. Both --analytics and --refresh-topics now print the hint string they are about to send so the loop is visible from the CLI. --- Hook Formulas Every script uses one of 5 proven hook formulas chosen by Claude for that specific event: | Formula | Example | |---|---| | SHOCKINGFACT | "A man once sold the Eiffel Tower — twice." | | FALSEASSUMPTION | "Everyone thinks Einstein failed math. He didn't — but his teachers still wanted him gone." | | CONSEQUENCEFIRST | "This one telegram started World War One." | | SPECIFICNUMBER | "In 1518, 400 people danced non-stop for 2 months — and couldn't stop." | | DIRECTADDRESS | "You've used this invention today — but its creator was executed for making it." | Hard-banned openers: "Did you know", "In [year]...", any visual reference. Scripts now follow a 5-beat retention structure: Hook → Context → Rehook → Twist → Ending fact. The rehook is designed to reset curiosity midway through the short, and the ending fact is prompted to connect back to the opener for better loopability. Daily Automation (Windows Task Scheduler) Run --auto daily and --refresh-topics weekly via Windows Task Scheduler. See HOWTOUSE.md for the full setup guide. --- Image Generation (Priority Order) | Priority | Backend | Requirement | |---|---|---| | 1 | HuggingFace (FLUX.1-schnell) | HUGGINGFACEAPITOKEN in .env | | 2 | Replicate (FLUX.1-dev) | REPLICATEAPITOKEN in .env ($0.025/img) | | 3 | PIL placeholder | Always available (offline fallback) | Each image is retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff before falling back to the next backend. --- Voice Generation (Priority Order) | Priority | Backend | Requirement | |---|---|---| | 1 | ElevenLabs (hosted, highest quality) | ELEVENLABSENABLED=true + ELEVENLABSAPIKEY in .env (Starter $5/mo) | | 2 | Kokoro (open-weight neural TTS) | pip install kokoro>=0.9.4 soundfile + espeak-ng + Python 3.10–3.12 | | 3 | Piper TTS (local) | Binary on PATH | | 4 | Coqui TTS (local) | pip install TTS | | 5 | Edge TTS | Included in requirements.txt (always available fallback) | ElevenLabs sits at the top of the chain but is env-gated: it's only used when ELEVENLABSENABLED=true and a key is present, otherwise the pipeline falls back to Kokoro. See elevenlabs.md for the cost/decision record. Default Kokoro voice: bmgeorge (British Male) at KOKOROSPEED=1.1. Using ElevenLabs Set in .env (no code changes needed): env ELEVENLABSENABLED=true ELEVENLABSAPIKEY=... # from elevenlabs.io ELEVENLABSVOICEID=JBFqnCBsd6RMkjVDRZzb # "George" — British narrator ELEVENLABSMODEL=elevenmultilingualv2 # or elevenflashv25 (½ the credits) Customising Voice Set in .env — no code changes needed: env KOKOROVOICE=bmgeorge # afheart / amecho / bfemma / bmgeorge / amliam ... KOKOROLANGCODE=b # a=American EN, b=British EN, e=Spanish, f=French, h=Hindi, i=Italian, p=Portuguese KOKOROSPEED=1.1 # 0.5=slow · 1.1=default Shorts pacing · 1.5=fast > Voice and lang code must match — e.g. bmgeorge requires KOKOROLANGCODE=b. See HOWTOUSE.md for the full voice list. --- Scene Planning & Presets Between script generation and rendering, a lightweight scene planning layer converts each script into an explicit, inspectable ScenePlan. Each narrative beat becomes its own scene with a role-aware image prompt and its own duration. script → scene plan → image / render inputs → video assembly Videos are rendered as clean static slideshows — no zoompan/motion, and no on-screen text beyond the burned-in subtitles and the subscribe CTA in the final seconds. Scene roles The five semantic parts of every script each become a scene with a distinct visual treatment: | Role | Intent | |-----------|-------------------------------------------------| | hook | Strong, immediate establishing frame | | context | Explanatory, informative | | rehook | Mid-story curiosity reset | | twist | Heightened contrast / drama | | ending | Clean closing frame with negative space for CTA | Each scene carries: role, text, duration, imageprompt, and visualhints. Plans are saved to output/ /sceneplans/ .json and can be hand-edited between runs (the video step reads them back). Presets (--preset) Presets bundle per-role prompt-style tokens and duration weights. | Preset | Feel | |---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------| | documentaryclean | Archival, restrained palette (default) | | dramatichistory | Chiaroscuro, bold contrast, cinematic shadows | | viralfactcard | Saturated, TikTok-style punchy grading | bash python orchestrator.py --auto --preset dramatichistory python orchestrator.py --topic "Strange Moments" --keyword war --preset viralfactcard Omitting --preset uses config.DEFAULTSCENEPRESET (defaults to documentaryclean). All existing CLI flags continue to work unchanged. Extending - New preset — add a Preset to pipeline/presets.py and register it in PRESETS. It's picked up by --preset automatically. --- Output Format - Resolution: 1080×1920 (9:16 vertical) - Codec: H.264, AAC 128kbps, 24fps - Duration: 20–30 seconds - Subtitles: Burned in, white bold text, semi-transparent background box, positioned above YouTube Shorts UI. Whisper captions use shorter 3-word cards for faster pacing, while the estimation fallback keeps larger cards for smoother reading. - CTA Overlay: "Follow @ThatActuallyHappened11" — white text, top-center, appears in last 3 seconds - Thumbnail: auto-selected by YouTube from a video frame --- Output Structure output/ / events.json step 1 — discovered event scripts.json step 2 — script + SEO metadata + hooktype + scenevisuals + localizations (es/pt/hi/id) sceneplans/ step 2.5 — per-event ScenePlan JSON (role-aware scenes + prompts) images/ step 3 — one PNG per scene + imgN.txt sidecar with the exact prompt sent to the backend audio/ step 4 — narration WAV subtitles/ step 5a — .ass + .srt caption files video/ step 5b — assembled MP4 uploads.json step 6 — video IDs + URLs state.json per-step completion ledger topicsqueue.json topic queue with virality scores (local-only, git-ignored) videoregistry.json persistent record of all uploaded videos (local-only, git-ignored) logs/ daily rotating logs (14-day retention) assets/music/ drop royalty-free .mp3 files here for background music growth/ marketing strategy guides (Reddit strategy, etc.) --- Built With Claude Code This project was built entirely using Claude Code: - Agents — Plan agents for architecture design, Explore agents for codebase analysis, and general-purpose agents for parallelising research across multiple files simultaneously - Multi-session memory — persistent MEMORY.md tracking architecture decisions, tier completion status, and implementation patterns across all development sessions

    Description: Automates the creation of short AI-generated videos for social media (YouTube Shorts, Reels, TikTok) with script generation, video sourcing, voiceover, and upload.
    Language: Jupyter Notebook
    Topics: 

    README:
    AIVideoShortsGenerator - 100 % Free This Python script automates the creation of short AI-generated videos suitable for platforms like YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok. It takes a desired topic as input, generates a concise script using an LLM, finds relevant stock footage, creates a voiceover, edits the video with subtitles, and uploads it to specified social media platforms (currently YouTube and X are implemented for upload). Overview 🧐 The primary goal of this project is to streamline the process of creating engaging short videos for social media by: Generating compelling and concise video scripts based on a user-provided topic. Automatically sourcing relevant stock videos from Pixabay. Creating a natural-sounding voiceover for the script using a text-to-speech engine. Editing the video by merging the footage and voiceover, and adding dynamic subtitles. Providing functionality to automatically upload the generated video to YouTube Shorts and X. Technologies Used 💻 Python OpenAI (via OpenRouter): For generating free video scripts using a powerful language model (Deepseek) 🧠. Pixabay API: For sourcing royalty-free stock videos 🖼️. edge-tts: For generating free natural-sounding voiceovers 🗣️. MoviePy: For free video editing tasks, including merging audio and video, and adding subtitles 🎬. Tweepy: For uploading videos to X 🐦. Google API Client: For uploading videos to YouTube 📺. Other Libraries: pandas, numpy, librosa, soundfile, asyncio, etc. for various utilities. Key Features ✨ Automated Script Generation: AI-powered script creation tailored for short, engaging social media content. Automatic Video Sourcing: Fetches relevant stock footage from Pixabay based on the topic. Text-to-Speech Voiceover: Creates a natural-sounding voiceover for the generated script. Dynamic Subtitles: Adds stylized and dynamically positioned subtitles to the video. Video Editing: Combines the video, voiceover, and subtitles into a final video. Automated Upload: Implements functionality to directly upload the generated video to YouTube Shorts and X. Customizable Topic: Easily change the desiredtopic to create videos on various themes. Potential Improvements ✨ More Platform Support: Implement automated upload functionality for Instagram Reels and TikTok. Advanced Video Editing: Explore more sophisticated video editing techniques, transitions, and effects. Background Music: Add the option to include royalty-free background music. Visual Enhancements: Integrate more advanced visual elements and animations. Topic Generation: Automate the topic selection process. Contributing Contributions to this project are welcome. Feel free to fork the repository and submit pull requests with improvements or bug fixes.

    Language: Python

    README:
    📹 YouTube AI Content Generator An automated YouTube content generation system that creates videos using AI. This tool handles the entire content creation pipeline: from topic brainstorming to script writing, audio narration, image generation, video composition, and YouTube uploading. 🔍 Overview This project creates educational and philosophical content videos with minimal human intervention. It leverages several AI APIs to generate engaging content for YouTube. 📁 Project Structure . ├── audio/ # Generated audio files ├── images/ # Generated images for videos ├── resources/ # Assets for video creation │ ├── prompts/ # Text prompts for AI generation │ ├── font files # Typography for videos │ └── additional assets # Other resources ├── text/ # Generated text content ├── videos/ # Output video files ├── .env # Environment variables ├── browser.py # Browser automation utilities ├── clientsecrets.json # YouTube API credentials ├── datatovideo.py # Video composition module ├── history.json # Record of generated content ├── image.py # Image processing utilities ├── main.py # Main application entry point ├── portutils.py # Networking utilities ├── requirements.txt # Python dependencies ├── setup scripts # Configuration scripts ├── suggestions.json # Stored content suggestions ├── texttoaudio.py # Text-to-speech modules ├── texttoimage.py # Text-to-image generation modules ├── texttotext.py # Text content generation modules ├── token.json # API authentication tokens └── videotoyoutube.py # YouTube upload functionality ⚙️ Workflow 1. Topic Generation: Creates a random topic using the OpenAI or DeepSeek APIs 2. Script Creation: Generates a detailed script based on the topic 3. Audio Narration: Converts the script to spoken audio using ElevenLabs or Replicate 4. Image Prompt Generation: Creates descriptive prompts for visuals 5. Image Creation: Generates images using OpenAI or Replicate APIs 6. Thumbnail Creation: Designs an eye-catching thumbnail 7. Video Assembly: Combines images, audio, and text into a complete video 8. Run the Setup Script: - For Windows: sh setup.bat - For Unix-based systems: sh setup.sh ▶️ Running the Project Start the content generation process: - For Windows: sh start.bat - For Unix-based systems: sh start.sh The script will continuously generate and upload videos based on the configured workflow. 📝 Note This code isn't perfect and may require adjustments based on your specific needs and API changes. However, it successfully achieves the core job of automating content creation from concept to published video. 📄 License This project is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Modes | Command | Mode | Background | |---------|------|------------| | python app.py skeleton | Anatomy facts | skeleton/ folder | | python app.py trending | Trending topics | Pexels API | | python app.py challenge | 30-day list format | gameplay/ folder | | python app.py cinematic skeleton | AI scenes + Ken Burns | Pollinations AI | | python app.py cinematic skeletor | Skeletor progression | Pollinations AI | | python app.py cinematic socrates | Socrates funny situations | Pollinations AI | | python app.py cinematic chad | Chad transformation | Pollinations AI | Quick Start bash pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # fill in GROQAPIKEY at minimum python app.py skeleton Environment Variables GROQAPIKEY= # required for all modes PEXELSAPIKEY= # optional, only for 'trending' mode YOUTUBECHANNELID= # optional, only for auto-upload Footage Setup (optional — improves quality) - skeleton/ — drop anatomy/skeleton .mp4 clips here - gameplay/ — drop Minecraft/Subway Surfers clips here - music/ — drop background music .mp3 files here - assets/fonts/Anton-Regular.ttf — download free from Google Fonts How Cinematic Mode Works 1. A video URL, a topic, your own script or a GitHub/Hugging Face page becomes a publish-ready video in any niche - with an original song or a cloned voiceover, a lip-synced presenter, captions, a thumbnail and SEO metadata, then one-click upload.
    Language: Python
    Topics: ai, animation, comfyui, fastapi, ffmpeg, generative-ai, kids-content, llm, music-generation, pipeline, python, self-hosted, seo, text-to-video, thumbnail-generation, tts, video-generation, vllm, whisper, youtube

    README:
    VideoGen — AI Video Generator for Your YouTube Channel VideoGen turns a YouTube video, a topic, your own script or a GitHub / Hugging Face page into a brand-new AI video tailored to one of your channels — animated, realistic or tech-explainer, with content rules matching the channel's audience — complete with an original soundtrack or a voiceover narration in a voice you choose (Fish Speech voice cloning), scene-synced visuals, a YouTube-ready thumbnail, and SEO metadata — then publishes it to YouTube with one click, using locally hosted AI services end to end. Pick a channel, give it a URL, a topic or your own script, choose an art style and aspect ratio, and the pipeline produces a finished final.mp4 plus everything needed to publish it. Finished videos can then be joined into one long compilation — chapters, title and thumbnail included — which is where a channel's watch time actually comes from. Features - Four ways to create a video — a YouTube URL (transcript-driven), a topic (the LLM invents the script), your own description / short script (the LLM builds on it faithfully), or a pasted transcript / script (used as the script as-is; the LLM only fixes typos, cue tags and the like). Kids-channel song videos can additionally take your own song lyrics, sung verbatim. Topic/description/transcript jobs draft their script immediately — outside the video queue — and wait for your approval before any video generation starts. - Bring your own music — on a song video, upload a track (10 seconds to 6 minutes) instead of having one generated. It is used as the soundtrack exactly as you recorded it, no song is written or rendered, and the video comes out the same length as your music: the track's measured duration decides how many clips are made. Any vocals are transcribed once so the scenes follow what is sung; a purely instrumental track gets scenes that follow the script instead. Available on any channel. - 30 selectable art styles — Anime, Western Cartoon, Pixar-like 3D, Claymation, Watercolor, and more; each drives the visual direction of every generated shot and the thumbnail. A preview image of each style (rendered once by your own video model via Settings → "Generate style previews") is shown while picking. - Multiple channels — manage any number of channels in Settings, each with its own name, purpose, logo, audience (Kids / Family / General), video type (Animated / Real / Tech / DIY build shorts) and per-video defaults. Every video is generated to match the channel picked in the New Video dialog, and uploads go to that channel's own connected YouTube account. Real and Tech channels skip the art-style picker and use a built-in realistic live-action look; Tech channels additionally get concrete, technically accurate scripts (devices, screens, code, data-centre visuals) and the on-screen story board switched on by default. - DIY build shorts — a channel type for the fast, vertical "watch him build it" format: the channel's recurring builder makes one project, from bare materials to the finished reveal, in one fixed backyard or workshop, cut between wide shots and hand close-ups. The voiceover is a quick third-person play-by-play that opens on a curiosity hook question ("Why would anyone put PVC pipes on a post?"), walks through the steps and lands on why it is clever. It plays over a light instrumental bed and the clips' own work sounds (drills, soil, water), and nothing is written on screen. A new DIY channel defaults to 9:16, 30-45 seconds and voiceover + music, renders on LTX 2.5 (its clips carry sound), and uses the builder's portrait as a likeness reference that never appears on screen. Clips are DIYCLIPSECONDS long (3 s) for the quick cutting, the voice is sped up by DIYNARRATIONTEMPO, and uploads are filed under Howto & Style. - On-screen story board — an optional overlay (per video, default on for Tech channels) of styled fact cards: the LLM plans a kicker (KEY FACT, HOW IT WORKS, BY THE NUMBERS…), a headline and a one-line body for the right moments of the narration, some with a related still image rendered by the video model in a shape matching the video (square for portrait, 4:3 for square, 16:9 for landscape); the cards are drawn with Pillow and composited over the clips with fades, timed to the actual clip cuts. A card never shares the screen with the hook or the end card, and on a repository video it yields a few tenths of a second to the page panel rather than crowding it out. Toggle or regenerate it on any finished job, then reassemble. - Eight card layouts, several in every video — a video no longer shows the same rectangle six times. Each card's own content picks a layout family — a card carrying a figure becomes a big stat (the number pulled out as the hero) or a compact accent chip; a card with a rendered still becomes a split or an overlapping photo stack; the opening and closing cards become a centred full-bleed banner or a quote slab; everything else is the classic lower third or an edge-to-edge ribbon. A seed taken from the job id picks the variant inside the family, so the mix never repeats a layout back to back and the same job always renders identically — a reassemble, an upscale or a regenerated clip can never restyle a finished video, because each card's layout is frozen into plan.json the first time it is planned. Cards also ease into place instead of only fading in, which costs nothing: the movement is a per-frame position in the overlay pass that already runs, so it is still one encode. Settings offers the full mix, a panels-only set, or classic-only. - Burned-in captions — word-synced subtitles over the video, with the word being spoken picked out in colour. Controlled at three levels: a master switch in Settings (off means no video is captioned, whatever anything else asks for, and reassembling an existing video strips them), a per-channel default, and a per-video switch in the New Video dialog. Default on for Tech channels. The words come from the script itself, not from a transcription of it: the narration is timed with whisper and then snapped back onto the written text, so a mis-heard word is corrected before it is ever drawn. Story videos need no transcription at all — every line is spoken on its own and laid on the clip grid, so its timings are exact by construction — and song videos reuse the timings already made for the lyric-synced scenes. The track is an .ass subtitle file burned by libass in the same encode as the overlays, so captions cost no extra pass, and it carries the frame size so it scales itself to whatever resolution the video was upscaled to. A caption never sits on a story board card: for as long as one is up, the caption moves above it. - A presenter who speaks the voiceover — the narration no longer has to come from nowhere. Give a channel a roster of portraits on the Settings page, pick which one speaks a video, and that face is animated to lip-sync the narration and composited over the clips: either a cut-out with no background, anchored to the bottom edge so the torso runs off frame (a floating head with a cut neck is the thing that looks wrong), or a circle bubble in a corner with a ring and a drop shadow. It appears over the intro and the outro by default — the middle belongs to the story board — and the windows are snapped to the gaps between spoken words, reusing the caption timings the pipeline already has, so a segment never starts or stops mid-syllable. Whole video lays the segments end to end instead: on an engine that renders a fixed chunk (Wan: 4.75 s) that is a contiguous chain of them, one render per chunk — and each chunk after the first is conditioned on the tail of the one before it, so the presenter carries his pose and gesture across the seam instead of snapping back to the portrait. That chaining has a cost that only shows on a long take: each chunk continues the picture of the last one, not just its pose, so small deviations from the uploaded face compound and past roughly 30-40 seconds of one unbroken chain the presenter is recognisably someone else. So the chain is re-anchored every few chunks - AVATARCHAINMAX, four by default - by rendering that chunk from the portrait alone, which costs a visible pose change at that one seam and keeps nothing more than three hops from the photograph. Every chunk of an appearance also renders on one seed derived from the job id, rather than fresh noise each time: with the portrait pinned as the reference either way, new noise per chunk made the model re-read the same face at every seam, and it made two runs impossible to compare. The overlay stops fading there too: a chain fades in once at its start and out once at its end, and is drawn at one size throughout, rather than every chunk fading to nothing and being re-fitted on its own. It falls back to the two bookends when the budgets cannot pay for the whole length, which is what they are there to decide. Two engines, chosen per video: Wan 2.2 S2V holds the likeness (the face in the video is recognisably the person you uploaded) and is the default, while LTX 2.5 is 33x faster and already the stack the clips render on, so it is what a tight budget falls back to — it lip-syncs about as well but renders a younger, thinner stranger. Neither was picked by eye: both were correlated against the speech envelope, with a time-reversed envelope as the control. Because the good engine costs 9 s of GPU per output frame, two budgets guard it — how much presenter a viewer should see (AVATARMAXSECONDS) and how much of the shared GPU one video may spend getting it (AVATARMAXRENDERMINUTES) — and coverage is trimmed to fit with the reason logged, never silently. Both budgets, the look, the size and the corner are on the Settings page; size and position are read at assembly time, so changing them and reassembling applies to a finished video without re-rendering a frame. Cutting the background away runs on your CPU, not the GPU box, because matting is cheap (0.7 s a frame) and the render box is a shared, serial resource better spent on the render. The portrait is prepared once, when you upload it — flattened opaque and cropped square anchored on the head rather than the image centre, so no per-video time goes into it and a tall headshot never loses the top of its head. Placement is computed from fractions of the frame, so one setting covers 1080p through 4K and 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1 alike, and the overlay is drawn in the same single encode as the cards and captions. A missing portrait, a missing model or a blown budget costs the overlay and nothing else — the video is still finished. - Two thumbnails when there is a presenter — a video with a talking-head avatar also gets its thumbnail with the presenter in it: one frame of the segment, cut out with the matte already made for the overlay, composited into the same corner at the same fraction of the frame the video uses, so the thumbnail promises the picture the video delivers. Both versions are offered on the job page — with the face and without, each with its text treatments and a text-free option — because which one earns the click is a judgement call and neither costs a GPU render. Automatic whenever the video has a presenter; a failure costs only that extra choice. - A thumbnail that carries text — the generated picture still contains no letters (image models spell badly, and the prompt forbids typography), so a punchy 3-5 word line is drawn over it afterwards with Pillow, in three different treatments. One GPU render, three candidates: pick one on the job page and it becomes the thumbnail the download, the publish bundle and the YouTube upload all use. "No text" stays a choice. Controlled the same three ways as the captions — a master switch in Settings, a per-channel default and a per-video switch — except that it defaults on for every channel, not just Tech ones: it is drawn on the thumbnail image rather than over the video. Works retroactively — a video made before this existed adopts its own finished thumbnail as the base. On a kids channel the line is cut to 2-3 words under 18 characters instead of 5 under 24, and the picture is composed for a toddler audience being scrolled past on a phone: one character's face filling most of the frame, at most one other object, a flat high-contrast background, no scenery and nothing in the distance. Five small words and a busy background read as noise at thumbnail size, which is the likeliest reason a channel sits at 2.7% click-through against the 4-7% kids content should reach. The length the model is asked for and the length the drawing enforces come from one place, so they cannot drift apart. - Real tags, the right category and chapters — the SEO step always generated search keywords and then threw them away, so every upload went out with no tags at all; they are now packed under YouTube's 500-character cap and sent. Uploads were also hard-coded to category 24 (Entertainment), which buries a technical video: a Tech channel is now filed under 28 (Science & Technology). And the description gains a chapter list built from the real clip cut points, obeying YouTube's rules exactly (first at 0:00, at least three, each at least ten seconds) — a video too short for a valid list simply gets none, because YouTube ignores a partial one. - Hook card, end card and progress bar — the opening line is already the first thing spoken; it is now also shown full-screen over the first seconds, which is the whole video for a viewer who has not pressed unmute. A subscribe card closes the video, kept clear of the lower-right quarter where YouTube draws its own end-screen elements, and a thin accent progress bar fills across the bottom. A short whoosh marks each card appearing — synthesized with ffmpeg on first use and cached, so no audio file ships with the app — and it is deliberately not ducked under the voice, since a whoosh you cannot hear while the narrator talks is pointless. The final mix is also loudness-normalised to about -14 LUFS, which is what YouTube normalises to anyway: an un-normalised master is simply played quiet. - Clean voiceover mix — voiceover videos mix narration + an instrumental bed only: the clips' own generated sound effects are dropped by default (they clashed with the voice and the music and jumped at every cut; CLIPAUDIOWITHMUSIC brings them back). The music bed is side-chain ducked under the voice, looped with a cross-fade when the model ends the track early, faded out at the end, and the mix is trimmed to the video and soft-limited. When ambience is kept it is dipped to silence around every clip cut. - Audience-aware safety — the channel's audience preset drives the LLM content rules: kids channels stay strictly gentle and family-friendly (even "dark" styles render playful and reassuring), family channels allow mild peril, general channels follow platform guidelines only. - Channel branding — each channel's name replaces any channel/brand names found in source content, across narration, lyrics, and SEO; its purpose text steers the tone of every script. - Character videos on or off — a per-channel switch on the Settings page. On, the channel's recurring cast drives every script, scene, thumbnail and weekly plan. Off, the channel makes informative explainers instead: hook, the viewer's problem, the concrete steps, the payoff, spoken straight to the viewer as "you" — no protagonist, no story, no invented persona. Generic unnamed people (a project manager at a laptop, hands typing, a presenter) can still appear on screen, they are just never named or recurring. It is independent of the audience preset, so a grown-up channel can have characters and a kids channel could go character-free. Switching it off keeps the cast and its portraits, so it is reversible. - Videos from a GitHub repo or a Hugging Face model — on a Tech channel, paste a github.com repository or a huggingface.co model, dataset or space URL instead of a YouTube link. The README or model card and the project's real facts (stars, downloads, licence, task, library) become the script, which you review and approve before anything renders. Optionally the live page is screenshotted with a locally installed headless Chrome and scrolled slowly as a large panel over the middle of the video, so viewers see the actual repo. The panel keeps its window even when the story board cards fill the middle — the cards are shortened to clear it, which costs about 0.3 s of one card — while the hook and end cards are never covered. No extra Python packages; if no browser is found the video is still made from the README. - The video keeps its promises — when a script offers the viewer something ("the exact prompt structure is in the description", "grab the checklist"), that thing is written and saved with the video as resource.md, resource.txt and a branded resource.pdf carrying the channel logo, and appended to the generated YouTube description so it is ready to publish. The decision comes from the finished script alone and the promise has to be quoted out of it word for word, so a video that promises nothing gets nothing. The script writer is never told to make such an offer. - Every repo video ships a setup guide — a video made from a GitHub repo or a Hugging Face page always hands the viewer the hands-on guide for that project, whether or not the script promised anything, because the README it was written from already holds the install and quickstart material. Requirements, install commands, first run, the flags worth knowing and a short troubleshooting list, written from that README only — never from what the model remembers about the project — and saved as the same three files, with the channel logo and name on the PDF and the channel name over the text versions. It is a download, not a description append: nobody was told to look in the description for it, so the SEO description is left exactly as written. A script that did promise something still wins, so a video never ships two documents. - Recurring cast — give a channel up to 24 named characters (an elephant, a kid, …) with a precise look and personality, or import a Character Bible (a markdown document with a ### Name block per character plus style, rules and checklist sections) in one paste on the Settings page: the character blocks become cast entries, the other sections become the channel's Style & rules text that is sent as a fixed reference with every script and scene prompt. Not every character is in every video: the LLM picks the 1-3 the story needs (or exactly the ones you name in the topic, e.g. "Use Ava as the main character and Leo as the supporting character"); the full roster is only sent while the script is written, afterwards every prompt carries just this video's characters, and each character's canonical look is prepended to every scene, thumbnail and story board prompt that names them, so the video model gets the same description every time. Approve a reference portrait per character (rendered by your video model in the channel's art style, or uploaded): the first character of the story that has one becomes the first frame of clip 1, so the video opens on the real character and the following clips chain from it. Looks and colours stay consistent; faces can still drift later in long videos, since the model has no identity-lock beyond the first frame. - Rank the cast by what actually performs — a channel's characters are never equally popular: on this one the top character earned 50 hours of watch time and the weakest earned six minutes, yet every one of them was equally likely to be cast. Each character now carries a priority on the Settings page — Lead (carries the channel), Normal, or Resting (don't cast) — separate from its role, because a flagship character and a dud can both be "main". Leads are listed first in the roster the script writer sees and are the ones it is told to cast; a resting character is left out unless you name it yourself in the topic, which still works. The weekly planner spends most of the week on the leads, and whatever reaches for "the first character" — the portrait that opens a video, the faces in a thumbnail — reaches for a lead. It is set by hand, deliberately: the app's YouTube permission is upload-only and cannot read your analytics, so you paste in what you see in Studio. A resting character keeps its portrait, its voice and its canonical look, so nothing you already made changes and the decision is reversible; a channel that never touches the field keeps exactly the prompts it had. A character bible may also carry a Priority: line. - Job dashboard — the jobs list shows every job's parameters at a glance (channel, audio choice and voice, art style, target length, aspect ratio, clip progress), with a per-channel filter, text search and pagination; the archive page gets the same filter, search and pagination. - Song or voiceover, chosen per video — the New Video dialog offers Generate Song (an original song is generated first; its actual length sets the clip count and its lyrics drive the visuals) or Generate Voiceover (the LLM writes the narration, Fish Speech speaks it, and a gentle instrumental music bed — never sung lyrics — is mixed underneath at low volume). The channel's default audio preselects the dialog; a pure narration mode (no music bed) remains available via the API. - Voice cloning with reference voices — upload short speech samples (plus the exact text spoken in them) on the Settings page, then pick a voice per voiceover video; Fish Speech clones it for the narration. No selection = the model's default voice, kept the same for the whole video (the first narration chunk becomes the reference for the rest, so long narrations no longer switch speakers between chunks); a random voice per segment option keeps the old behaviour. - Sing your own lyrics (kids channels) — the New Video dialog shows an optional Song lyrics box when a kids channel is set to Generate Song. Paste a sheet and those exact words are sung: the LLM only writes the music caption and adds [Verse]/[Chorus] tags, and a deterministic check puts your words back if it edited any. Your lyrics also set the length — Video length greys out, the target is your sung-word count at the kids singing pace, and the “too short” rewrite never runs. Up to 250 sung words. - Compilations — one long video out of the finished ones — pick 2 to 12 finished videos of a channel on the Jobs page and they become a single long upload, in the order you tick them. This exists because of what a channel's own numbers say: a short video has to find its own audience and most never do, while one ten-minute compilation on this channel produced a quarter of its entire watch time, and watch time is what the recommendation surfaces actually run on. Nothing is rendered — the videos are joined exactly as they were finished, so a twenty-minute compilation is a minute of local ffmpeg, never queued behind a render and never waiting for the GPU window. It gets a chapter list with one chapter per video, at the real cut it starts on and titled with that video's own title; a title that opens with the length ("18 Minutes of Tilly the Train | Toddler Songs & Stories" — rounded down, because a title promising more than it delivers is the one inaccuracy a viewer punishes immediately) and a description written for the compilation; and a thumbnail lifted from one of its parts, with the usual three text treatments drawn over it, so the whole job costs no GPU render at all. It is an ordinary job from there on: upload it to YouTube with one click, download the bundle, upscale it, archive it. The parts stay published in their own right and a compilation keeps playing even if one of them is later deleted. Videos of different sizes are fitted and padded to the largest frame among them rather than cropped (a part may already be published, so losing its edges is worse than a black border); mixing portrait and landscape in one compilation is refused rather than decided badly. A week of planned videos also offers "Make a compilation from this week" once its videos are done, which opens the picker with exactly those videos already ticked. - Weekly planner — the Planner page writes a week of video ideas for one channel in a single LLM call: 2 to 7 dated rows, spaced out across the week rather than stacked on its first days, because every upload competes with the channel's others for the same audience — a few strong videos plus a compilation beats a daily trickle. Asking for fewer also changes what is written, not just how much: the brief tells the LLM these are the week's best ideas, each worth a full watch, rather than handing back the same seven minus four. Seven stays the default, and a plan made before this existed still reads as the seven-day week it was. Each row carries the cast it needs, a title, a 2-4 sentence story from beginning to end, a thumbnail idea and the spoken opening line. Earlier titles from that channel are sent along so a new week never repeats one. Rewrite any day you do not like (with optional feedback), then confirm the rows you want — each becomes a paused job that runs nothing until you open it and press Start. On a kids channel with a cast you can pick Video type → Story based for the whole week, and every video confirmed from it arrives already set up as a story, so a week of stories is one choice rather than seven. The plan remembers that choice, and the week is written knowing it — a story is rendered as clips that each continue from the previous one, so its ideas stay in one or two connected places instead of hopping across the world. - Story videos (kids channels) — a per-video Video type choice next to the audio options: Song based (everything above) or Story based. A story video is the other way round from a song: the LLM first invents the scenes that build the story — one beat per clip, each a single visible action in a place the previous beat can walk into — and only then writes the voiceover from those beats. That order is the whole feature. The spoken lines are nothing but what happens and what the characters say (“Ellie waited for the train to arrive.”, “All aboard!”), never a description of the picture: the writer is never even shown the character looks, a worked wrong/right example is in the prompt, and a deterministic check catches any line that still names a colour, a garment, a species or the camera and has just that line written again. Every character speaks in its own voice — give each cast member a reference voice on the Settings page, or set one default character voice for the channel (a child sample makes the whole channel sound like kids); a character with neither gets a voice invented once and kept for the whole video. Each line is spoken on its own and laid out on the clip grid, so the picture and the words are in sync by construction — no transcription, no alignment. A clip is the usual length, or longer when its line needs the room, and you review and edit every scene and line before anything renders. - Lyric-accurate visuals — the generated song is transcribed with word timestamps (faster-whisper); each clip's scene is written from the words actually sung during that clip's window, so what you hear is what you see. Instrumental passages get atmosphere/transition scenes. - Two video models, chosen per video — clips render on either MiniMax H3 or LTX 2.5. Pick the default on the Settings page and override it per video in the New Video dialog (or a planned job's setup card); the jobs list, the archive and the job page all badge which model a video used. The two round clip length differently — a requested 5 s comes out as 5.17 s on H3 and 5.04 s on LTX — and that real length is what the lyric windows, the story line timing and the clip count are built from, so the choice is frozen when the video is planned: it cannot be switched under a job whose audio is already laid out. LTX 2.5 also takes a negative prompt, which defaults by channel type (naming cartoon and video-game looks helps a Real/Tech channel and fights an animated one) and is editable in Settings. Thumbnails, cast portraits and story board stills always render on MiniMax H3 whatever a video picked — they are 5-frame renders, a length only that graph can express. Adding a third model is one entry in config.VIDEOMODELS plus its workflow JSON: no node id lives anywhere else. - Continuous clips — clip 1 is text-to-video; every following clip is seeded with the last frame of the previous one for smooth visual flow. Both models ship a text-to-video and a first-frame graph, so the chaining works the same either way. - Thumbnail generation — an LLM-designed scene that instantly shows what the video is about, rendered through the video model as a JPG matching the video aspect ratio (1280×720 for 16:9, 720×1280 for portrait, etc.), with the channel's logo overlaid top-right. One-click regeneration on any finished job. - SEO metadata — a keyword-optimized YouTube title and description (with hashtags and a subscribe call-to-action) generated for every video. On a kids channel the title rule is different, because a toddler-content title is not read but scanned — by a parent typing two or three words into the search box, and by a sidebar that truncates around 60 characters on a phone: the words that get the video found have to come first. The title is capped at 60 characters with the character's name and the plain subject ("Train", "Clean Up Song", "Learn Colors", "ABCs") inside the first 40, and it may never open with the channel name, a number or a clause before the subject. The weekly planner writes its titles in that same shape, so the SEO pass sharpens them instead of fixing them. Every other audience keeps the original rule. - LLM review pass — every generated scene and every drafted script is reviewed a second time by the LLM against the exact audio/content it must match, and inconsistencies (a wrong letter, a mismatched object, an unsafe detail) are fixed automatically. The reviewer is transcription-aware: if the speech recognizer misheard a letter, it trusts the word ("fairy" belongs to F). Toggleable via SCRIPTREVIEW. - Per-job target length — pick Auto, 30-45 s, 45-60 s, 1-2 min, 2-3 min, 3-4 min or 4-5 min when creating a job; a soft target that guides the script length and the generated song/narration duration (ignored when you supply your own song lyrics — those set the length instead). A song that lands short of the range is rewritten longer and re-rendered once, and a script drafted well under its word target is extended before it is spoken. Longer targets also render longer clips (up to 10 s), so a 5-minute video is about 27 clips rather than 59. - One-click YouTube upload — connect each channel to its own YouTube account (OAuth, youtube.upload scope only) and push any finished video straight to that channel with live progress: uploaded private by default (review in YouTube Studio before publishing), with the SEO title/description, the made-for-kids flag (a per-channel toggle), and custom thumbnail applied. Connecting works from a remote server too: Google's localhost redirect is completed by pasting its address into a dialog, or set a Public base URL with a Web-type client on an HTTPS domain for a fully automatic sign-in. One-time Google Cloud setup guide: docs/YOUTUBE.md. - Title-named downloads & bundle — the video and thumbnail download as .mp4 / .jpg, and one click grabs the whole publish bundle: a ZIP with the video, any upscaled versions, thumbnail, audio track(s), and the SEO title/description in a text file. - Output resolution & on-demand upscaling — pick 1080p / 2K / 4K per video (or as the Settings default) to have the final video upscaled during assembly, or upscale a finished video later from its job page; every version is kept separately. - Full revision workflow — edit any scene prompt in the UI, regenerate exactly the clips you want (they're clearly badged), then reassemble the final video with one click. Regenerations jump the queue, pausing the running job at a clip boundary and resuming it afterwards. - Robust operations — crash-safe resume (every pipeline step is idempotent), instant cancel (including aborting the in-flight GPU render), a two-lane queue over one GPU (only generation is serial — the next job writes its script and times its words while this one renders) with live status messages, automatic ComfyUI server cleanup (per artifact, plus an orphan sweep at startup and after every job that catches renders left behind by retries or crashes), transcript quality gating, and a self-restarting server watchdog. - Login and user accounts — the whole app sits behind a sign-in screen. On the very first start a one-time setup page creates the administrator account; it never appears again. Channels and videos are per user: each user creates and manages their own channels and sees only their own videos; admins see every user's channels and videos (tagged with the owner, with an owner filter), are the only ones who can change the service settings, GPU schedule, reference voices, style previews and users, and inherit the channels and videos of accounts they delete. Everyone can change their own password. Sessions are signed cookies (30 days); passwords are stored as scrypt hashes in users/ (never committed). - Polished web UI — dark/light theme, a New Video dialog behind a Create new video button, a type-to-search art-style picker with live model-rendered previews, search across the Jobs and Archived Jobs lists, configurable dialog defaults, live progress with a pipeline stepper, rich per-job detail pages, archive/cancel/delete, and a runtime Settings page with service health checks.
